# 4414 in 2026: storage, a compact turret and an entire operating policy

RIPCURRENT is useful as an architecture case because its components reinforce each other. The low singulator, small turret swept volume, chassis shape, storage walls, net and movable collection system allocate the same scarce interior space. Merely writing “turret with a big hopper” loses the reason the package is interesting. The base dossier and the team’s interactive binder describe the construction; this supplement adds the team’s explanations of calibration, autonomy, geometry and iteration. [Interactive technical binder](https://2026.team4414.com/). [Discussion](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602).

## Preserve the terms before reasoning from them

The relevant singulator reference is DYE Rotor, a paintball-loader family. It should not be parsed as “di-rotor,” an assertion that there are two rotors, or a generic synonym for any spindexer. The architecture has to be identified from its actual feed paths and independent drives. Likewise a turret makes azimuth independent of chassis heading within its usable range; it does not by itself establish accuracy at every location, continuous firing under every acceleration or immunity to defense.

The current reviewed capacity claims in the binder are 85+ fuel in the trench-capable configuration and 100+ with the net over the bump. The user’s 110-fuel example remains unverified in this edition. A 110-inch frame-perimeter reference must not be turned into 110 stored fuel. An additional later measurement could resolve that question, but a persuasive narrative is not a substitute for it. Capacity also needs a defined condition: static fill, retained fuel while moving, fuel actually deliverable to the shooter and a particular net/deployment configuration can all differ.

## The geometry is a system-level choice

The base dossier records the compact turret, the large low rotor, chamfered chassis, offset battery packaging and structural storage walls. The team later describes an early inspiration that changed its thinking from a square machine toward a wider chamfered shape. This is evidence of design lineage, not a claim that the exact inspirational sketch was fabricated. [October reflection](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/157).

A useful agent generalization is that reducing an assembly’s swept volume can be worth more than making its standalone performance better. A smaller turret can leave more storage around it, permit a better floor route and reduce the space needed for wiring. Those gains can increase how long the robot remains useful in a scoring shift. But the tradeoff must be tested: a compact shooter may have poorer compression consistency, less flywheel inertia, more difficult service or a tighter hood path. The geometry only wins if the integrated robot delivers more reliable output under the target conditions.

The published images include separate rotor V1–V10 and shooter V1–V11 asset labels. These are preserved in the gallery. Some filenames mention pre-Ventura, Ventura or Orange County; the other V-numbers should not be assigned to event configurations without further evidence. An image of a prototype is evidence that a design was considered or published, not that it survived qualification, played at Worlds or ran simultaneously with every other pictured part.

## Do not copy the successful calibration story without the empirical part

The team says its shot solver drew from 1690’s 2022 presentation, but searched a region of shots reaching the near and far rim rather than only targeting the center. It chose solutions with tolerance to exit-speed and angle error. The team then measured angle offset and empirically calibrated exit speed against commanded wheel speed; one shooter revision needed a nonlinear lookup. It frames the benefit as reducing tuning effort, while explicitly not claiming the season’s best shot or best shooting on the move. [Shot-model explanation](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/116).

The independent engineering implication is to model uncertainty, not only nominal trajectories. Ball wear, contact state, feeder speed and wheel compression can change actual exit conditions. If an architecture relies on a computed trajectory but cannot measure or repeat the exit state, adding more aerodynamic terms may not solve its dominant error. Conversely, a well-designed mechanism can make a compact empirical calibration useful across many conditions. An agent should recommend an experiment that identifies the dominant uncertainty before recommending a more complicated simulator.

For a different shooter, the transferable goal is a maintainable calibration procedure. That procedure should say what changes when fuel ages, when a wheel is replaced, when the feed geometry is adjusted and when a hood reference drifts. It should also say how the team distinguishes a localization error from an exit-velocity error. Otherwise a driver can lose an entire event chasing the wrong tuning parameter.

## Vision hardware and the hardware that actually worked are different records

The team describes a turret-mounted Limelight using MegaTag 1 and supplementary USB cameras on an Orange Pi. Historical gyro and turret angles are buffered so camera observations can be transformed at their measurement time before filtering and fusion. The team reports no precise absolute turret zero, using a visually approximated starting zero and accepting a small consequence for the gyro reference. It calls that a local prioritization decision. [Vision account](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/107).

The team separately says it ran Champs eliminations with only one working camera on the Orange Pi after USB-port failures, with ESD offered as a suspected explanation. This establishes the difference between intended sensor architecture and the functional configuration in an important competition period; it does not prove the electrical failure mechanism. [Functional configuration](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/111).

This case should therefore not become an agent rule that absolute sensing is unnecessary or that any one camera platform is inherently unreliable. The useful lesson is that the target’s tolerance, the observation geometry and the team’s familiarity can change the value of a more rigorous reference system. A different game with narrow placement or multi-target tasks can expose errors that a large hub did not. An architecture recommendation needs both nominal performance and degraded operation when a camera, port or reference fails.

## A lower peak autonomous routine can be a better alliance routine

The team explains testing depot-auto variants and finding that double swipes left insufficient time to fire and reach the desired transition position. It preferred crossing the bump once to improve compatibility and avoid being affected if a partner got stuck. The chosen path also depended on a fuel triangle that did not reliably form without enough robots rushing midfield. [Autonomous tradeoff](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/124).

That dependency should remain attached to the recommendation. A routine optimized for four strong midfield contestants may collect less at a sparse local event or with a different opponent plan. Similarly, a transition endpoint has value because of what the robot can do next, not because “center” is universally optimal. The agent should compare complete auto-plus-transition outcomes under several partner/opponent configurations, including an obstruction and a failed pickup. Scoring more in the first interval can lose more in the next interval if the machine ends in a poor location with an empty hopper.

## Collision recovery is part of useful throughput

The team reports changing the bottom plastic from 1/16 to 1/8 inch after weight became available, and finding that the stiffer sheet helped the robot slide off fuel. The same reply describes an unsuccessful camera-wiring experiment that damaged hardware. Both belong in the record, but neither should be copied as a generic recipe. [Packaging and belly-sheet account](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/105).

This matters strategically because a robot with lower nominal firing rate can outperform a faster one if it spends less time stranded, realigning or hunting for a feedable pile. The correct comparison is fuel successfully scored during useful windows, including the time needed to acquire, transfer, aim, recover and return. It should be measured against representative defense and fuel distribution. A claim that this turret “almost outscored the best drums” needs an identified match, the other robots’ roles and the relevant scoring conditions; this edition does not turn that phrase into a universal ranking of mechanism families.

## What a recommendation inspired by RIPCURRENT should contain

Recommend the package when independent aiming, mobile collection and storage preservation match the team’s intended role and development capacity. State the cost in singulator development, calibration, wiring, sensor recovery and service access. Compare it against a braced fixed shooter with a simpler floor and a wide drum under the same supply and defense assumptions. Prototype partially depleted and mixed-load feeding, not just a full static hopper. Keep a dated configuration record for every claimed improvement. The available evidence is strong enough to make RIPCURRENT a useful source of architectural ideas; it is not complete enough to certify every intermediate competition version, the user’s exact 110-fuel number or a guaranteed advantage against any named drum.


# 2026-4414: technical mechanisms, design reasoning and revision boundaries

These notes distinguish published construction from team-stated intent and original engineering inference. Selected numerical values are reported source data, not independently reproduced measurements. The recommended tests have not been performed. A binder snapshot does not certify every competition version.

## RIPCURRENT: shape the chassis and bumpers around the feed system

Version: 4414 RIPCURRENT interactive technical binder. [Technical source](https://2026.team4414.com/)

**Published construction:** Chamfered 25×32-inch base; offset battery rail; structural bumper/hopper walls and low electronics.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Preserve low rotor diameter and storage area within the perimeter.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A singulator occupies a swept area, not just a rectangular bounding box. Changing chassis corners can preserve the parts of that area that most improve ring diameter while removing less useful perimeter. Moving the battery to an edge creates a new structural problem because the rail still has to carry drive and impact loads. Using the bumper backing as a hopper boundary can reclaim interior width, while tying scorer alignment to a removable impact structure. The package needs a repeatable bumper interface, and the stored-fuel center of mass must be evaluated alongside the empty robot.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Reinstall bumpers and measure scorer alignment; test loaded lateral acceleration and rotor clearance after representative impacts.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## RIPCURRENT: independently driven rotor, packing relief and passive contact

Version: 4414 RIPCURRENT interactive technical binder. [Technical source](https://2026.team4414.com/)

**Published construction:** Separate rotor/feed drives; shaped fin and wrap guides; passive rollers and omni contacts.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Reduce packing pressure, friction and belt slip.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A bulk pile can load the singulator even when the exit path is clear. Agitating the pile and supplying the launch stream are different motions, so separating drives gives useful tuning freedom. A shaped fin can alter where that pile pressure is released; passive rollers reduce sliding resistance where balls push against each other. These details explain why a DYE-inspired design cannot be generalized as a generic circular indexer. The critical behavior is the changing network of contacts at full, partial and nearly empty loads, including a controlled reverse to clear a bridge.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure stream continuity and current at several load states; observe whether agitation increases entry occupancy or merely recirculates fuel.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## RIPCURRENT: compliant racks and a separately latched lower contact

Version: 4414 RIPCURRENT interactive technical binder. [Technical source](https://2026.team4414.com/)

**Published construction:** Stacked polycarbonate racks; primary and lower powered rollers; strengthened hubs and shear interfaces.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Impact compliance and reliable pickup with retained storage.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Stacking plates can create controlled flex only if the plates and fasteners permit the intended relative motion. A low roller that remains deployed adds another ownership contact near the bumper, while its latch removes continuous holding load from an actuator. Stronger hubs and distributed shear interfaces address local failure modes that a thicker arm alone may not fix. The collector also moves storage boundaries, so its success must be measured while the hopper is loaded and the side walls are being pushed by fuel.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test diagonal wall contact, rack synchronization and lower-latch retention; inspect roller-end alignment and capacity after impact.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## RIPCURRENT: compact shooter swept volume and stored energy

Version: 4414 RIPCURRENT interactive technical binder. [Technical source](https://2026.team4414.com/)

**Published construction:** Four-X44 3-inch flywheel; added dense inertia; powered hood roller; vertically stacked motor package.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Reduce protrusions while preserving the desired launch contact.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A compact turret can improve the whole robot by leaving more feed and storage volume around its swept envelope. That benefit must be weighed against launch-contact repeatability, motor cooling, wire access and flywheel recovery. Dense inertia stores energy in limited space, but increases spin-up energy and bearing loads. A powered hood contact changes the spin state and must remain geometrically consistent as the hood moves. The key comparison with a drum is delivered scored fuel during usable windows, including time moving and acquiring, rather than a single instantaneous output rate.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Map exit velocity and spin versus hood angle, turret heading and volley length; inspect belt tracking under acceleration.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## RIPCURRENT: calibration and uncertainty remain empirical

Version: 4414 RIPCURRENT interactive technical binder. [Technical source](https://2026.team4414.com/) · [Team explanation](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/116)

**Published construction:** Team reply describes robust-shot selection followed by measured angle and velocity calibration.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Choose trajectories tolerant of exit-state errors.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A nominal ballistic solution is not enough when fuel compression, wear and launch contact change the actual exit velocity. Searching for a region of successful trajectories can improve tolerance, but the model must be anchored to measurements of the real mechanism. Separate localization, hood-reference and exit-speed errors before retuning: otherwise one correction can conceal another. This is a transferable technical procedure, not evidence that every team should adopt the same equation set or that the robot can score under every motion and defense condition.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Use stationary known-pose tests to isolate launch error, then add translation, rotation and tilt one at a time.

**Limits:** Construction is from the previously reviewed binder and current indexed binder text; calibration explanation is from team reply /519602/116. Current direct binder download returned 403. Existing source images were retained; no new visual watching is claimed.

dossier.narrative_context:
# 4414 in 2026: storage, a compact turret and an entire operating policy

RIPCURRENT is useful as an architecture case because its components reinforce each other. The low singulator, small turret swept volume, chassis shape, storage walls, net and movable collection system allocate the same scarce interior space. Merely writing “turret with a big hopper” loses the reason the package is interesting. The base dossier and the team’s interactive binder describe the construction; this supplement adds the team’s explanations of calibration, autonomy, geometry and iteration. [Interactive technical binder](https://2026.team4414.com/). [Discussion](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602).

## Preserve the terms before reasoning from them

The relevant singulator reference is DYE Rotor, a paintball-loader family. It should not be parsed as “di-rotor,” an assertion that there are two rotors, or a generic synonym for any spindexer. The architecture has to be identified from its actual feed paths and independent drives. Likewise a turret makes azimuth independent of chassis heading within its usable range; it does not by itself establish accuracy at every location, continuous firing under every acceleration or immunity to defense.

The current reviewed capacity claims in the binder are 85+ fuel in the trench-capable configuration and 100+ with the net over the bump. The user’s 110-fuel example remains unverified in this edition. A 110-inch frame-perimeter reference must not be turned into 110 stored fuel. An additional later measurement could resolve that question, but a persuasive narrative is not a substitute for it. Capacity also needs a defined condition: static fill, retained fuel while moving, fuel actually deliverable to the shooter and a particular net/deployment configuration can all differ.

## The geometry is a system-level choice

The base dossier records the compact turret, the large low rotor, chamfered chassis, offset battery packaging and structural storage walls. The team later describes an early inspiration that changed its thinking from a square machine toward a wider chamfered shape. This is evidence of design lineage, not a claim that the exact inspirational sketch was fabricated. [October reflection](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/157).

A useful agent generalization is that reducing an assembly’s swept volume can be worth more than making its standalone performance better. A smaller turret can leave more storage around it, permit a better floor route and reduce the space needed for wiring. Those gains can increase how long the robot remains useful in a scoring shift. But the tradeoff must be tested: a compact shooter may have poorer compression consistency, less flywheel inertia, more difficult service or a tighter hood path. The geometry only wins if the integrated robot delivers more reliable output under the target conditions.

The published images include separate rotor V1–V10 and shooter V1–V11 asset labels. These are preserved in the gallery. Some filenames mention pre-Ventura, Ventura or Orange County; the other V-numbers should not be assigned to event configurations without further evidence. An image of a prototype is evidence that a design was considered or published, not that it survived qualification, played at Worlds or ran simultaneously with every other pictured part.

## Do not copy the successful calibration story without the empirical part

The team says its shot solver drew from 1690’s 2022 presentation, but searched a region of shots reaching the near and far rim rather than only targeting the center. It chose solutions with tolerance to exit-speed and angle error. The team then measured angle offset and empirically calibrated exit speed against commanded wheel speed; one shooter revision needed a nonlinear lookup. It frames the benefit as reducing tuning effort, while explicitly not claiming the season’s best shot or best shooting on the move. [Shot-model explanation](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/116).

The independent engineering implication is to model uncertainty, not only nominal trajectories. Ball wear, contact state, feeder speed and wheel compression can change actual exit conditions. If an architecture relies on a computed trajectory but cannot measure or repeat the exit state, adding more aerodynamic terms may not solve its dominant error. Conversely, a well-designed mechanism can make a compact empirical calibration useful across many conditions. An agent should recommend an experiment that identifies the dominant uncertainty before recommending a more complicated simulator.

For a different shooter, the transferable goal is a maintainable calibration procedure. That procedure should say what changes when fuel ages, when a wheel is replaced, when the feed geometry is adjusted and when a hood reference drifts. It should also say how the team distinguishes a localization error from an exit-velocity error. Otherwise a driver can lose an entire event chasing the wrong tuning parameter.

## Vision hardware and the hardware that actually worked are different records

The team describes a turret-mounted Limelight using MegaTag 1 and supplementary USB cameras on an Orange Pi. Historical gyro and turret angles are buffered so camera observations can be transformed at their measurement time before filtering and fusion. The team reports no precise absolute turret zero, using a visually approximated starting zero and accepting a small consequence for the gyro reference. It calls that a local prioritization decision. [Vision account](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/107).

The team separately says it ran Champs eliminations with only one working camera on the Orange Pi after USB-port failures, with ESD offered as a suspected explanation. This establishes the difference between intended sensor architecture and the functional configuration in an important competition period; it does not prove the electrical failure mechanism. [Functional configuration](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/111).

This case should therefore not become an agent rule that absolute sensing is unnecessary or that any one camera platform is inherently unreliable. The useful lesson is that the target’s tolerance, the observation geometry and the team’s familiarity can change the value of a more rigorous reference system. A different game with narrow placement or multi-target tasks can expose errors that a large hub did not. An architecture recommendation needs both nominal performance and degraded operation when a camera, port or reference fails.

## A lower peak autonomous routine can be a better alliance routine

The team explains testing depot-auto variants and finding that double swipes left insufficient time to fire and reach the desired transition position. It preferred crossing the bump once to improve compatibility and avoid being affected if a partner got stuck. The chosen path also depended on a fuel triangle that did not reliably form without enough robots rushing midfield. [Autonomous tradeoff](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/124).

That dependency should remain attached to the recommendation. A routine optimized for four strong midfield contestants may collect less at a sparse local event or with a different opponent plan. Similarly, a transition endpoint has value because of what the robot can do next, not because “center” is universally optimal. The agent should compare complete auto-plus-transition outcomes under several partner/opponent configurations, including an obstruction and a failed pickup. Scoring more in the first interval can lose more in the next interval if the machine ends in a poor location with an empty hopper.

## Collision recovery is part of useful throughput

The team reports changing the bottom plastic from 1/16 to 1/8 inch after weight became available, and finding that the stiffer sheet helped the robot slide off fuel. The same reply describes an unsuccessful camera-wiring experiment that damaged hardware. Both belong in the record, but neither should be copied as a generic recipe. [Packaging and belly-sheet account](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/105).

This matters strategically because a robot with lower nominal firing rate can outperform a faster one if it spends less time stranded, realigning or hunting for a feedable pile. The correct comparison is fuel successfully scored during useful windows, including the time needed to acquire, transfer, aim, recover and return. It should be measured against representative defense and fuel distribution. A claim that this turret “almost outscored the best drums” needs an identified match, the other robots’ roles and the relevant scoring conditions; this edition does not turn that phrase into a universal ranking of mechanism families.

## What a recommendation inspired by RIPCURRENT should contain

Recommend the package when independent aiming, mobile collection and storage preservation match the team’s intended role and development capacity. State the cost in singulator development, calibration, wiring, sensor recovery and service access. Compare it against a braced fixed shooter with a simpler floor and a wide drum under the same supply and defense assumptions. Prototype partially depleted and mixed-load feeding, not just a full static hopper. Keep a dated configuration record for every claimed improvement. The available evidence is strong enough to make RIPCURRENT a useful source of architectural ideas; it is not complete enough to certify every intermediate competition version, the user’s exact 110-fuel number or a guaranteed advantage against any named drum.

technical_notes.title: RIPCURRENT: shape the chassis and bumpers around the feed system
technical_notes.construction: Chamfered 25×32-inch base; offset battery rail; structural bumper/hopper walls and low electronics.
technical_notes.team_stated_reason: Preserve low rotor diameter and storage area within the perimeter.
technical_notes.engineering_analysis: A singulator occupies a swept area, not just a rectangular bounding box. Changing chassis corners can preserve the parts of that area that most improve ring diameter while removing less useful perimeter. Moving the battery to an edge creates a new structural problem because the rail still has to carry drive and impact loads. Using the bumper backing as a hopper boundary can reclaim interior width, while tying scorer alignment to a removable impact structure. The package needs a repeatable bumper interface, and the stored-fuel center of mass must be evaluated alongside the empty robot.
technical_notes.recommended_validation: Reinstall bumpers and measure scorer alignment; test loaded lateral acceleration and rotor clearance after representative impacts.
technical_notes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test. This is a cross-revision feature overview, not a single certified configuration. technical_notes.title: RIPCURRENT: independently driven rotor, packing relief and passive contact
technical_notes.construction: Separate rotor/feed drives; shaped fin and wrap guides; passive rollers and omni contacts.
technical_notes.team_stated_reason: Reduce packing pressure, friction and belt slip.
technical_notes.engineering_analysis: A bulk pile can load the singulator even when the exit path is clear. Agitating the pile and supplying the launch stream are different motions, so separating drives gives useful tuning freedom. A shaped fin can alter where that pile pressure is released; passive rollers reduce sliding resistance where balls push against each other. These details explain why a DYE-inspired design cannot be generalized as a generic circular indexer. The critical behavior is the changing network of contacts at full, partial and nearly empty loads, including a controlled reverse to clear a bridge.
technical_notes.recommended_validation: Measure stream continuity and current at several load states; observe whether agitation increases entry occupancy or merely recirculates fuel.

technical_notes.title: RIPCURRENT: compliant racks and a separately latched lower contact
technical_notes.construction: Stacked polycarbonate racks; primary and lower powered rollers; strengthened hubs and shear interfaces.
technical_notes.team_stated_reason: Impact compliance and reliable pickup with retained storage.
technical_notes.engineering_analysis: Stacking plates can create controlled flex only if the plates and fasteners permit the intended relative motion. A low roller that remains deployed adds another ownership contact near the bumper, while its latch removes continuous holding load from an actuator. Stronger hubs and distributed shear interfaces address local failure modes that a thicker arm alone may not fix. The collector also moves storage boundaries, so its success must be measured while the hopper is loaded and the side walls are being pushed by fuel.
technical_notes.recommended_validation: Test diagonal wall contact, rack synchronization and lower-latch retention; inspect roller-end alignment and capacity after impact.

technical_notes.title: RIPCURRENT: compact shooter swept volume and stored energy
technical_notes.construction: Four-X44 3-inch flywheel; added dense inertia; powered hood roller; vertically stacked motor package.
technical_notes.team_stated_reason: Reduce protrusions while preserving the desired launch contact.
technical_notes.engineering_analysis: A compact turret can improve the whole robot by leaving more feed and storage volume around its swept envelope. That benefit must be weighed against launch-contact repeatability, motor cooling, wire access and flywheel recovery. Dense inertia stores energy in limited space, but increases spin-up energy and bearing loads. A powered hood contact changes the spin state and must remain geometrically consistent as the hood moves. The key comparison with a drum is delivered scored fuel during usable windows, including time moving and acquiring, rather than a single instantaneous output rate.
technical_notes.recommended_validation: Map exit velocity and spin versus hood angle, turret heading and volley length; inspect belt tracking under acceleration.

technical_notes.construction: Team reply describes robust-shot selection followed by measured angle and velocity calibration.
technical_notes.team_stated_reason: Choose trajectories tolerant of exit-state errors.

context_documents.body:
> Revision correction 2026-11-07: [Read all ten rotor and eleven shooter prototypes](../2026-4414_REVISION_HISTORY.md). Earlier feature summaries below span multiple versions; their specifications do not apply to every prototype. Event installation and cross-family pairing remain unknown.

# 4414 in 2026: storage, a compact turret and an entire operating policy

RIPCURRENT is useful as an architecture case because its components reinforce each other. The low singulator, small turret swept volume, chassis shape, storage walls, net and movable collection system allocate the same scarce interior space. Merely writing “turret with a big hopper” loses the reason the package is interesting. The base dossier and the team’s interactive binder describe the construction; this supplement adds the team’s explanations of calibration, autonomy, geometry and iteration. [Interactive technical binder](https://2026.team4414.com/). [Discussion](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602).

## Preserve the terms before reasoning from them

The relevant singulator reference is DYE Rotor, a paintball-loader family. It should not be parsed as “di-rotor,” an assertion that there are two rotors, or a generic synonym for any spindexer. The architecture has to be identified from its actual feed paths and independent drives. Likewise a turret makes azimuth independent of chassis heading within its usable range; it does not by itself establish accuracy at every location, continuous firing under every acceleration or immunity to defense.

The current reviewed capacity claims in the binder are 85+ fuel in the trench-capable configuration and 100+ with the net over the bump. The user’s 110-fuel example remains unverified in this edition. A 110-inch frame-perimeter reference must not be turned into 110 stored fuel. An additional later measurement could resolve that question, but a persuasive narrative is not a substitute for it. Capacity also needs a defined condition: static fill, retained fuel while moving, fuel actually deliverable to the shooter and a particular net/deployment configuration can all differ.

## The geometry is a system-level choice

The base dossier records the compact turret, the large low rotor, chamfered chassis, offset battery packaging and structural storage walls. The team later describes an early inspiration that changed its thinking from a square machine toward a wider chamfered shape. This is evidence of design lineage, not a claim that the exact inspirational sketch was fabricated. [October reflection](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/157).

A useful agent generalization is that reducing an assembly’s swept volume can be worth more than making its standalone performance better. A smaller turret can leave more storage around it, permit a better floor route and reduce the space needed for wiring. Those gains can increase how long the robot remains useful in a scoring shift. But the tradeoff must be tested: a compact shooter may have poorer compression consistency, less flywheel inertia, more difficult service or a tighter hood path. The geometry only wins if the integrated robot delivers more reliable output under the target conditions.

The published images include separate rotor V1–V10 and shooter V1–V11 asset labels. These are preserved in the gallery. Some filenames mention pre-Ventura, Ventura or Orange County; the other V-numbers should not be assigned to event configurations without further evidence. An image of a prototype is evidence that a design was considered or published, not that it survived qualification, played at Worlds or ran simultaneously with every other pictured part.

## Do not copy the successful calibration story without the empirical part

The team says its shot solver drew from 1690’s 2022 presentation, but searched a region of shots reaching the near and far rim rather than only targeting the center. It chose solutions with tolerance to exit-speed and angle error. The team then measured angle offset and empirically calibrated exit speed against commanded wheel speed; one shooter revision needed a nonlinear lookup. It frames the benefit as reducing tuning effort, while explicitly not claiming the season’s best shot or best shooting on the move. [Shot-model explanation](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/116).

The independent engineering implication is to model uncertainty, not only nominal trajectories. Ball wear, contact state, feeder speed and wheel compression can change actual exit conditions. If an architecture relies on a computed trajectory but cannot measure or repeat the exit state, adding more aerodynamic terms may not solve its dominant error. Conversely, a well-designed mechanism can make a compact empirical calibration useful across many conditions. An agent should recommend an experiment that identifies the dominant uncertainty before recommending a more complicated simulator.

For a different shooter, the transferable goal is a maintainable calibration procedure. That procedure should say what changes when fuel ages, when a wheel is replaced, when the feed geometry is adjusted and when a hood reference drifts. It should also say how the team distinguishes a localization error from an exit-velocity error. Otherwise a driver can lose an entire event chasing the wrong tuning parameter.

## Vision hardware and the hardware that actually worked are different records

The team describes a turret-mounted Limelight using MegaTag 1 and supplementary USB cameras on an Orange Pi. Historical gyro and turret angles are buffered so camera observations can be transformed at their measurement time before filtering and fusion. The team reports no precise absolute turret zero, using a visually approximated starting zero and accepting a small consequence for the gyro reference. It calls that a local prioritization decision. [Vision account](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/107).

The team separately says it ran Champs eliminations with only one working camera on the Orange Pi after USB-port failures, with ESD offered as a suspected explanation. This establishes the difference between intended sensor architecture and the functional configuration in an important competition period; it does not prove the electrical failure mechanism. [Functional configuration](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/111).

This case should therefore not become an agent rule that absolute sensing is unnecessary or that any one camera platform is inherently unreliable. The useful lesson is that the target’s tolerance, the observation geometry and the team’s familiarity can change the value of a more rigorous reference system. A different game with narrow placement or multi-target tasks can expose errors that a large hub did not. An architecture recommendation needs both nominal performance and degraded operation when a camera, port or reference fails.

## A lower peak autonomous routine can be a better alliance routine

The team explains testing depot-auto variants and finding that double swipes left insufficient time to fire and reach the desired transition position. It preferred crossing the bump once to improve compatibility and avoid being affected if a partner got stuck. The chosen path also depended on a fuel triangle that did not reliably form without enough robots rushing midfield. [Autonomous tradeoff](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/124).

That dependency should remain attached to the recommendation. A routine optimized for four strong midfield contestants may collect less at a sparse local event or with a different opponent plan. Similarly, a transition endpoint has value because of what the robot can do next, not because “center” is universally optimal. The agent should compare complete auto-plus-transition outcomes under several partner/opponent configurations, including an obstruction and a failed pickup. Scoring more in the first interval can lose more in the next interval if the machine ends in a poor location with an empty hopper.

## Collision recovery is part of useful throughput

The team reports changing the bottom plastic from 1/16 to 1/8 inch after weight became available, and finding that the stiffer sheet helped the robot slide off fuel. The same reply describes an unsuccessful camera-wiring experiment that damaged hardware. Both belong in the record, but neither should be copied as a generic recipe. [Packaging and belly-sheet account](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/105).

This matters strategically because a robot with lower nominal firing rate can outperform a faster one if it spends less time stranded, realigning or hunting for a feedable pile. The correct comparison is fuel successfully scored during useful windows, including the time needed to acquire, transfer, aim, recover and return. It should be measured against representative defense and fuel distribution. A claim that this turret “almost outscored the best drums” needs an identified match, the other robots’ roles and the relevant scoring conditions; this edition does not turn that phrase into a universal ranking of mechanism families.

## What a recommendation inspired by RIPCURRENT should contain

Recommend the package when independent aiming, mobile collection and storage preservation match the team’s intended role and development capacity. State the cost in singulator development, calibration, wiring, sensor recovery and service access. Compare it against a braced fixed shooter with a simpler floor and a wide drum under the same supply and defense assumptions. Prototype partially depleted and mixed-load feeding, not just a full static hopper. Keep a dated configuration record for every claimed improvement. The available evidence is strong enough to make RIPCURRENT a useful source of architectural ideas; it is not complete enough to certify every intermediate competition version, the user’s exact 110-fuel number or a guaranteed advantage against any named drum.

> Revision correction 2026-11-07: [Read all ten rotor and eleven shooter prototypes](../2026-4414_REVISION_HISTORY.md). Earlier feature summaries below span multiple versions; their specifications do not apply to every prototype. Event installation and cross-family pairing remain unknown.

# 2026-4414: technical mechanisms, design reasoning and revision boundaries

These notes distinguish published construction from team-stated intent and original engineering inference. Selected numerical values are reported source data, not independently reproduced measurements. The recommended tests have not been performed. A binder snapshot does not certify every competition version.

## RIPCURRENT: shape the chassis and bumpers around the feed system

Version: 4414 RIPCURRENT interactive technical binder. [Technical source](https://2026.team4414.com/)

**Published construction:** Chamfered 25×32-inch base; offset battery rail; structural bumper/hopper walls and low electronics.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Preserve low rotor diameter and storage area within the perimeter.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A singulator occupies a swept area, not just a rectangular bounding box. Changing chassis corners can preserve the parts of that area that most improve ring diameter while removing less useful perimeter. Moving the battery to an edge creates a new structural problem because the rail still has to carry drive and impact loads. Using the bumper backing as a hopper boundary can reclaim interior width, while tying scorer alignment to a removable impact structure. The package needs a repeatable bumper interface, and the stored-fuel center of mass must be evaluated alongside the empty robot.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Reinstall bumpers and measure scorer alignment; test loaded lateral acceleration and rotor clearance after representative impacts.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## RIPCURRENT: independently driven rotor, packing relief and passive contact

Version: 4414 RIPCURRENT interactive technical binder. [Technical source](https://2026.team4414.com/)

**Published construction:** Separate rotor/feed drives; shaped fin and wrap guides; passive rollers and omni contacts.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Reduce packing pressure, friction and belt slip.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A bulk pile can load the singulator even when the exit path is clear. Agitating the pile and supplying the launch stream are different motions, so separating drives gives useful tuning freedom. A shaped fin can alter where that pile pressure is released; passive rollers reduce sliding resistance where balls push against each other. These details explain why a DYE-inspired design cannot be generalized as a generic circular indexer. The critical behavior is the changing network of contacts at full, partial and nearly empty loads, including a controlled reverse to clear a bridge.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure stream continuity and current at several load states; observe whether agitation increases entry occupancy or merely recirculates fuel.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## RIPCURRENT: compliant racks and a separately latched lower contact

Version: 4414 RIPCURRENT interactive technical binder. [Technical source](https://2026.team4414.com/)

**Published construction:** Stacked polycarbonate racks; primary and lower powered rollers; strengthened hubs and shear interfaces.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Impact compliance and reliable pickup with retained storage.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Stacking plates can create controlled flex only if the plates and fasteners permit the intended relative motion. A low roller that remains deployed adds another ownership contact near the bumper, while its latch removes continuous holding load from an actuator. Stronger hubs and distributed shear interfaces address local failure modes that a thicker arm alone may not fix. The collector also moves storage boundaries, so its success must be measured while the hopper is loaded and the side walls are being pushed by fuel.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test diagonal wall contact, rack synchronization and lower-latch retention; inspect roller-end alignment and capacity after impact.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## RIPCURRENT: compact shooter swept volume and stored energy

Version: 4414 RIPCURRENT interactive technical binder. [Technical source](https://2026.team4414.com/)

**Published construction:** Four-X44 3-inch flywheel; added dense inertia; powered hood roller; vertically stacked motor package.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Reduce protrusions while preserving the desired launch contact.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A compact turret can improve the whole robot by leaving more feed and storage volume around its swept envelope. That benefit must be weighed against launch-contact repeatability, motor cooling, wire access and flywheel recovery. Dense inertia stores energy in limited space, but increases spin-up energy and bearing loads. A powered hood contact changes the spin state and must remain geometrically consistent as the hood moves. The key comparison with a drum is delivered scored fuel during usable windows, including time moving and acquiring, rather than a single instantaneous output rate.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Map exit velocity and spin versus hood angle, turret heading and volley length; inspect belt tracking under acceleration.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## RIPCURRENT: calibration and uncertainty remain empirical

Version: 4414 RIPCURRENT interactive technical binder. [Technical source](https://2026.team4414.com/) · [Team explanation](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/116)

**Published construction:** Team reply describes robust-shot selection followed by measured angle and velocity calibration.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Choose trajectories tolerant of exit-state errors.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A nominal ballistic solution is not enough when fuel compression, wear and launch contact change the actual exit velocity. Searching for a region of successful trajectories can improve tolerance, but the model must be anchored to measurements of the real mechanism. Separate localization, hood-reference and exit-speed errors before retuning: otherwise one correction can conceal another. This is a transferable technical procedure, not evidence that every team should adopt the same equation set or that the robot can score under every motion and defense condition.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Use stationary known-pose tests to isolate launch error, then add translation, rotation and tilt one at a time.

**Limits:** Construction is from the previously reviewed binder and current indexed binder text; calibration explanation is from team reply /519602/116. Current direct binder download returned 403. Existing source images were retained; no new visual watching is claimed.

## Selected published parameters

| Component | Source parameter | Locator |
|---|---|---|
| Intake | 3-in main; 3.45:1; 1.5-in lower; 1.5:1 | [Source](https://2026.team4414.com/) |
| Rotor | 2.5:1 feeder; 36.4:1 rotation | [Source](https://2026.team4414.com/) |
| Shooter | 3-in flywheel; four X44s 1:1; 85.3:1 hood | [Source](https://2026.team4414.com/) |
| Turret | 55.7:1; constant-force cable tensioner | [Source](https://2026.team4414.com/) |

Ratios preserve source notation; verify driver/driven order, complete geometry and the actual version in CAD before fabrication. Figure records retain PDF page and crop bounds in `data/mechanism_images.jsonl`. Images may include rejected prototypes or whole-robot photographs; their captions preserve that distinction.

source_reviews.title: HighTide 2026 Technical Binder
source_reviews.locator: Dye Rotor, Intake, Shooter, Software and prototype gallery
source_reviews.review_basis: Read team-authored content in the published site JavaScript bundle
source_reviews.facts: Documents powered and passive contacts, packing relief, coupled hopper design, compact shooter packaging and trajectory computation.
source_reviews.limitations: Feature descriptions are published configuration summaries and should not be projected onto all gallery versions.

source_reviews.title: RIPCURRENT engineering release discussion
source_reviews.review_basis: Read original team-authored text via Discourse JSON
source_reviews.facts: Supplies explicit event version mapping, bumper removal support path, shot tuning and shared block CAD workflow.
source_reviews.limitations: The event account does not prove every intermediate test outcome or binary deployment.

source_review.whole_robot_explanation: RIPCURRENT uses a wide linear collector and a large hopper to gather fuel, then feeds a low rotating shooter through the Dye Rotor. The design concentrates the hard problem at the rotor: bulk inventory needs to reach a narrow vertical path without wedging and without obstructing the turret. The team’s published packaging preserves both a high-volume bin and a limited shooter sweep. Its event history shows the rotor and shooter evolved at different rates. The newer team reply establishes their event pairings, while the older gallery review remains useful for visible comparisons of the intermediate versions.
piece_flow: The linear collector uses an upper powered roller and a smaller lower powered roller that deploys between bumper gaps and stays down on latches.
Fuel settles around the rotor. A slowly counter-moving feature agitates the bed, contour prints guide fuel, and passive contacts lead into powered feeder wheels.
The compact turret accelerates a single stream. A driven hood contact, backing geometry and flywheel speed govern release while the turret supplies yaw.
source_review.packaging_and_motion: A chamfered base and bumper-integrated walls leave room for a large rotor. The team arranged shooter motors centrally and vertically, staggered plates to cut swept volume, and placed slim hood belts against the side plates. The turret bearing maintains support when the large bumper/hopper section is removed. The interference case includes the rotating hood, the deformable fuel bed and a trench crossing with stored fuel.

subsystems.name: Collector and hopper
subsystems.construction: Paired polycarbonate racks, powered upper and lower contacts, extending hopper and bumper-integrated walls.
subsystems.operation: Gather a wide swath and preserve containment when traveling.
subsystems.team_rationale: Team uses compliant rack layers and shaped impact guards for collection along field edges.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: Verify deployed geometry with side load and packed fuel. Two sides can deflect asymmetrically while the roller couples them.
subsystems.interfaces: Lower roller latches, intake extension and bumper geometry define the entry and service envelope.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: Inspect axle shear pins, latch engagement and rack travel after a corner hit.
subsystems.unknowns: Loaded wall shape and exact capacity by configuration.

subsystems.name: Dye Rotor and turret
subsystems.construction: Driven rotor and feed wheels, shaped contours and passive roller contacts. Four X44s on the published three-inch launcher flywheel with additional mass and a low-profile driven hood.
subsystems.operation: Agitate the bulk bed gently, then impose positive control through feed and release.
subsystems.team_rationale: Team sought reduced packing pressure, a smaller sweep and repeatable shots over a region of valid trajectories.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: A passive contact can let balls push one another through while reducing torque demand. Test whether it still turns freely under contamination.
subsystems.interfaces: Feeder alignment, turret bearing, hood belts and shot model depend on repeatable contact geometry.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: Check belt tracking, liner wear and rotor recovery with several pieces pushing against the exit.
subsystems.unknowns: Per-version compression maps and performance under current limits.

revisions: Team reports rotor V9 at Ventura, Orange County and district championship, then V10 at Worlds.
Team reports shooter V6 at Ventura, V8 at Orange County, V9 at district championship, and V11 at Worlds.
Earlier gallery documented ten rotor and eleven shooter renders. Team event mapping now resolves selected pairings without assigning an installation or outcome to every intermediate version.
transferable_principles: Set the packaging envelope before final detail. The team used shared block geometry to control collisions across independently developed subsystems.
Differentiate low-energy bulk agitation from controlled acceleration at the final nip.
Preserve a structural support path when removable hopper and bumper assemblies come off for inspection.
disconfirming_conditions: Rotating agitation can increase pressure at a narrowing exit if its direction, speed or geometry is mismatched to the packed bed.
A compact single stream can underperform a wide path when delivery rate or sensitivity to irregular fuel prevents sustained output.
Thin hood drives and tight stow gaps need a stiffness and impact margin. Nominal CAD clearance does not show the effect of bent parts.
remaining_gaps: No measured per-version jam rate, transfer current, shot conversion or complete prototype test history. Event mapping is team-reported and does not authenticate individual match installations.
recommended_images: Official binder isolated and powertrain views of the rotor and shooter. Gallery V9 and V10 rotor plus V6, V8, V9 and V11 shooter. Post 154 block CAD and post 116 shot-region plots.
